newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-StanChart - forex winner and loser.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-StanChart - forex winner and loser.

text.p: Standard Chartered, the bank based in London which gets almost all of its income from the Asia-Pacific region, saw its headline profit figures hit by translation into a strong pound after profiting significantly from Far East currency turmoil.
Chief Executive Malcolm Williamson told Reuters that the bank had not experienced such a big effect from translation into sterling before.

"The problem we have...is that we are very much a dollar-related bank, we either get our money in US dollars or currencies that are linked to it or currencies that have depreciated even more against sterling over the last year," Williamson said.
At constant exchange rates, the bank's trading profit rose by 16 percent but was only up a reported eight percent to 434 million stg compared to 402 million stg in the first half of 1996.
The bank used a sterling/dollar rate of 1.67 for the first half of this year, compared to 1.55 this time last year.
Williamson calculated that a rough rule of thumb is that StanChart loses around 50 million stg for every one percent change in the exchange rate.
But he pointed out that this was a rough calculation because the figures are affected both on the costs and income side and in the latter are affected by the mix of assets on the balance sheet.
StanChart was not only a loser because of currency fluctuations in the first half, however, because the bank profited strongly from currency volatility in the Far East.

Income from foreign exchange rose sharply to 108 million stg in the first half from 80 million stg in the same period last year, helping raise the bank's Treasury profits to 103 million stg from 76 million last time.
Williamson dismissed as "absolutely untrue" rumours in the foreign exchange markets that Standard Chartered had lost money in the volatility.
"We've had a very good record on this in the last few months," Williamson said. "You get daily ups and downs, but we've managed our book tightly and well and it's continued through July."
He said the financial turmoil in Thailand, Indonesia and Philippines had not affected the bank's business unduly.

While StanChart's exposure to the Thai property sector was nil small on a direct basis, Williamson said the bank had some counterparty exposure to Thai banks and finance houses and has made a special provision of five million pounds as a precaution.

"If you're big in a country, it's hard not to have some exposure, Williamson said. "Even though you yourself can keep your hands clean, the risk is that you get caught with some counterparty exposure with people who have been more profligate."
Standard Chartered said price competition for new lending in the Far East had been severe and saw its net interest margin edge lower to 3.4 percent from 3.5 percent.
Williamson said the bank had countered margin pressure in Hong Kong by going for growth in volumes and said that its business in Malaysia was also doing well.
Costs in the bank were higher, as it had flagged earlier, but income rose to a greater degree, leaving the cost to income ratio at 53.7 percent compared to 55.7 percent at the end of last year.
"The rise in costs is a question of putting resource where we really see the future," Williamson said.
On the income side, the biggest rise came from the Treasury operations but personal banking also produced good figures, increasing pre-provision profit by 16 percent.
StanChart shares were higher after the figures were announced, standing 28 pence higher at 1033.5p after reaching an earlier high of 1042p. -- Joe Ortiz, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8864.
